chapter_title: Organizing Gherkin Features: Tags, Hooks, and Backgrounds

screens.title: Organizing Gherkin Features: Tags, Hooks, and Backgrounds
screens.subtitle: Scale your executable specifications with labels, shared setup, and automation hooks

narration.text: When a project's feature files grow, organization becomes a testability and collaboration problem, not just a formatting choice. In this lesson you will learn three practical tools that keep your BDD suite readable and fast: tags for selective execution and categorization, Background sections for concise feature-level setup, and automation hooks for technical setup and teardown that live in code. I will show concrete examples you can apply immediately — a Gherkin tag to mark smoke tests, a Background that logs a user in before each scenario, and a Cucumber hook that initializes a browser only for UI-tagged scenarios. You will also see common pitfalls: overloading Background with too many steps, using hooks for business-domain setup that stakeholders should see, or scattering tags without a naming convention. By the end you will know when to prefer Background versus a code hook, how to use tags to speed CI pipelines, and simple structure choices that make features easier to maintain. Think about your current test suite: which repetitive step would you move into Background, and which technical initialization belongs in a hook?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use tags for selection, Background for feature-level readable setup, and hooks for technical global setup to keep tests maintainable and fast.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Organizing Gherkin Features
Organizing Gherkin Features
Tags, Backgrounds, and Hooks to keep BDD suites readable and scalable

This chapter teaches three coordination layers: human-readable feature setup (Background), execution and categorization (Tags), and technical automation (Hooks). Each layer has a distinct responsibility that avoids duplication and fragile tests.

Tags
Filter scenarios (@smoke, @regression), communicate intent, and target hooks.
Background
Put shared Gherkin steps that define a known state for every scenario.
Hooks
Code-level setup and teardown for resources or tagged scenarios.
Explore Key Topics
Tags: filter & categorize
Background: shared setup
Hooks: technical init/cleanup
Visual Concept
@smoke
Background: logged in
@Before("@ui") init browser
These cards represent the three layers working together: tags select scenarios, Background provides readable preconditions, and hooks perform technical steps triggered by tags.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical skills you'll use immediately. First, you will explain why organizing Gherkin matters when a test suite grows, and recognize how poor structure slows development and collaboration. Second, you'll learn to apply tags to features and scenarios so you can run targeted subsets of tests — for example, running smoke tests in CI after every commit. Third, you'll author Background sections that capture common, business-relevant preconditions so scenarios remain concise and readable to non-developers. Finally, you'll use hooks for technical setup and teardown, such as browser initialization and database cleanup, including how to scope those hooks by tag. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the separation of responsibilities between human-readable Background steps and code-based hooks. Throughout the exercises you'll practice a naming convention for tags and make a decision about what belongs in Background versus a hook. A useful rule of thumb to try: if the step is business-readable and important to stakeholders, keep it in Background; if it's technical infrastructure, put it in a hook. Which of your current tests will you reorganize first?

keyIdea.title: Objectives summary
keyIdea.text: Explain organization rationale, apply tags and Background, and implement hooks for technical setup to improve maintainability.

screens.title: Skills You Will Practice
screens.subtitle: Concrete actions and judgment calls for maintainable feature suites

narration.text: These practice goals help you convert principles into action. You will group features into domain folders so teammates can find them easily, and choose a tag naming convention to make automated selection predictable. You will move repeated human-facing steps into Background when they genuinely establish a known state for every scenario in a feature, and you will move technical initialization like opening a browser or clearing test data into hooks. You will also practice scoping hooks by tag so that only UI tests initialize a WebDriver, while A P I tests initialize a client. Each objective includes a verification step: run a filtered subset using tags, inspect the feature for repeated steps that belong in Background, and confirm that after adding hooks, resources are reliably cleaned up to avoid flakiness. A common misconception I will warn against is putting behavior that's part of a scenario into Background; that hides the scenario's intent. By practicing these actions you'll gain the judgment to keep BDD specifications both readable and executable.

screens.title: Tags: Labeling and Filtering Scenarios
screens.subtitle: How to use @tags to categorize, select, and drive conditional hooks

narration.text: Tags are lightweight labels prefixed with an at-sign that you can apply to Features, Scenarios, and Scenario Outlines. They are the primary mechanism for selecting which scenarios to run and for communicating intent. A common use is to mark critical user journeys with @smoke so CI runs them on each push, while @regression marks comprehensive suites run nightly. Tags also allow conditional hooks — a @Before("@ui") hook can initialize a browser only for UI tests. As a concrete example, imagine an authentication feature: tag the whole Feature with @authentication and individual scenarios with @smoke or @invalid_credentials. When you run the test runner with a tag expression such as "@smoke and not @wip" you run only critical scenarios that aren’t work-in-progress. A typical misconception is to treat tags as permissions or environment switches; they are declarative labels and should be used consistently. Another error is over-tagging every scenario differently; aim for a small set of orthogonal tags that reflect execution intent and domain area. Takeaway: choose a naming convention, document it, and use tags to speed CI feedback without hiding the feature’s behavior. Which tags can you add now to reduce runtime for your most frequent commits?

keyIdea.title: Tag usage
keyIdea.text: Tags categorize scenarios for selection and can trigger tagged hooks; keep tag sets small, meaningful, and consistent.

content.html:
Core Concept
Tags: Label & Filter
Tags allow fast selection and intent communication across features and scenarios.
Filtering: run a subset like --tags @smoke
Categorization: domain tags such as @authentication or @product
Conditional hooks: e.g., @Before("@ui") initialize browser
Example
@authentication @smoke
Feature: User Login
  Scenario: Successful login
    Given I am on the login page
    When I enter valid credentials
    Then I see the dashboard
Key Takeaway

Use tags to speed CI feedback and to scope hooks; adopt a small, documented tag set to avoid confusion.

Common mistakes & pro tip
Over-tagging
Giving each scenario unique tags defeats the purpose; prefer a few cross-cutting tags and domain tags.
Using tags as environment flags
Tags are labels about execution and intent, not feature toggles or runtime config switches.
Pro tip
Document tag semantics in a README so CI pipelines and team members use them consistently.

screens.title: Background: Shared Setup for Feature Files
screens.subtitle: When to use Background and how it affects scenario execution

narration.text: Background is a Gherkin section that runs before every scenario in a single feature file. Its purpose is to create a known state that every scenario expects, and to keep individual scenarios focused on the behavior they test. A concrete example: if every scenario in an account management feature requires the user to be logged in and on the account settings page, a Background with those steps removes repetition. It's important to keep Background concise: it should establish the precondition, not perform the action under test. A common misconception is placing the very behavior you are testing into Background; doing so hides the scenario's intent and can lead to misleading specifications. Another pitfall is adding too many steps to Background, which can slow execution and obscure which steps are relevant to which scenarios. To decide, ask: does this step represent a shared starting state for all scenarios in the feature? If yes, it belongs in Background. If not, keep it in each scenario. Takeaway: Background improves readability and reduces duplication when used for genuine shared setup. What repeated steps in your features would you move into Background without changing the scenarios' meanings?

keyIdea.title: Background rule
keyIdea.text: Use Background for shared, business-readable setup that should run before every scenario in a feature file; avoid hiding behavior.

content.html:
Definition
Background: shared preconditions
Background steps execute before each scenario in the same feature file and should express business-level setup that stakeholders understand.
Gherkin example
Feature: Account Management
  Background:
    Given I am logged in as "john.doe@example.com" with password "SecureP@ss"
    And I am on the "Account Settings" page

  Scenario: Update user profile information
    When I update my "first_name" to "Jonathan"
    Then my "first_name" should be "Jonathan"
When to use
When every scenario needs the same business state before it runs.
When not to use
Avoid placing the behavior under test into Background; that hides intent.
Key Takeaway

Background is for shared, readable preconditions. Keep it minimal to preserve clarity and speed.

Common mistakes
Too many steps
Overloading Background makes it hard to see which scenario actually tests what.
Hiding the behavior
If removing a Background step changes the scenario’s meaning, it probably belonged in the scenario, not the Background.
Pro tip
Review Backgrounds during refactoring to ensure they still represent shared state as features evolve.

screens.title: Hooks: Code-Level Setup and Teardown
screens.subtitle: Use hooks for global and tagged initialization and cleanup

narration.text: Hooks are automation framework methods that run before or after scenarios and are implemented in code. They are the correct place for technical setup such as starting a WebDriver, resetting a database connection, or taking screenshots on failure. Hooks can be global — running for every scenario — or tagged so they execute only for scenarios that match a tag expression. For example, a @Before("@ui") hook can initialize a browser only for UI tests, avoiding costly browser setup for A P I tests. A concrete example: use a @Before(order = 0) hook to configure environment state that other hooks depend on, and a later ordered hook to initialize a browser. Be careful to order hooks and perform cleanup in @After hooks so resources are released; failing to quit drivers or close DB connections causes leaks and flaky tests. A common misconception is putting stakeholder-visible setup in hooks instead of Background; that hides critical preconditions from non-technical readers. Takeaway: put technical concerns in hooks, keep business-readable setup in Background, and use tag-scoped hooks to make your suite efficient. Which technical initializations in your project should move into tagged hooks?

keyIdea.title: Hooks guideline
keyIdea.text: Use hooks for technical lifecycle work and scope them with tags and order to run only where needed and ensure cleanup.

content.html:
Process Flow
Hooks: before, after, ordered, and tagged
Hooks live in code and manage resources that are not part of the business narrative.
Typical responsibilities
  • Initialize and quit browser drivers
  • Open and close database connections
  • Take screenshots or collect logs on failure
Key Takeaway

Keep technical setup in hooks and business setup in Background. Use tag-scoped hooks to avoid unnecessary work.

Hook patterns
Global hooks
Run for every scenario to prepare or tear down shared resources.
Tagged hooks
Conditionally run setup only for scenarios that carry a specific tag such as @ui or @database.
Ordered hooks
Use order attributes to control execution sequence when multiple hooks exist.

screens.title: Cucumber Hooks Example (Java)
screens.subtitle: A simple Hooks class showing global and tagged hooks

narration.text: Let's walk through a concise Hooks implementation in Java for Cucumber. This example demonstrates a global @Before that runs first, a tagged @Before for database scenarios, and an @After that cleans up resources and conditionally takes a screenshot on failure. Read the visual code to understand the responsibilities: the global hook prepares shared infrastructure, the tagged hook configures feature-specific resources, and the after hook ensures resources are freed. A common misconception is that hooks should replicate business steps; they should not. Here the hooks only do technical tasks: setting system properties, initializing a driver, and closing it. As a concrete example, @Before("@database") could set up a test schema, while @Before(order = 0) runs base initialization first. Remember to null out references after quitting to avoid reusing stale drivers. Takeaway: hooks centralize and protect technical lifecycle tasks; use ordering and tags carefully to avoid resource contention. Which of these hooks would you add to your test suite to improve isolation? Cucumber Hooks Example (Java) means implement hooks for lifecycle concerns, order them for dependencies, and scope them by tag to avoid unnecessary work.. In practical terms, a simple hooks class showing global and tagged hooks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hooks in practice
keyIdea.text: Implement hooks for lifecycle concerns, order them for dependencies, and scope them by tag to avoid unnecessary work.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Hooks.java (example)
This example shows ordering, tagged hooks, and cleanup responsibilities in code.
Key Takeaway

Keep hooks focused on technical setup and teardown; avoid embedding business logic that belongs in Background or scenarios.

import io.cucumber.java.After;
import io.cucumber.java.Before;
import io.cucumber.java.Scenario;

public class Hooks {
  public static WebDriver driver;

  @Before(order = 0)
  public void setupBase() {
    System.out.println("Base setup for every scenario...");
    // e.g., system properties, shared test config
  }

  @Before("@database")
  public void setupDatabase() {
    System.out.println("Preparing database for @database scenario...");
    // create schema, seed data, or clear tables
  }

  @Before("@ui")
  public void setupBrowser() {
    System.out.println("Initializing browser for UI tests...");
    // driver = new ChromeDriver();
  }

  @After
  public void tearDown(Scenario scenario) {
    if (scenario.isFailed() && driver != null) {
      System.out.println("Scenario failed - taking screenshot...");
    }
    if (driver != null) {
      driver.quit();
      driver = null;
    }
  }
}

screens.title: Background vs Hooks: Choosing the Right Place
screens.subtitle: Contrast business-readable setup with technical initialization

narration.text: Distinguishing Background from hooks is essential for clarity and maintainability. Background belongs in feature files and expresses business-readable shared preconditions, for example, "Given I am logged in". Hooks belong in code and perform technical tasks such as starting a browser, clearing caches, or setting environment variables. A helpful rule: if a setup step is meaningful to stakeholders and relates to business behavior, prefer Background; if it is a technical detail that stakeholders do not need to see, use a hook. A common misuse is placing an important business precondition into hooks because it is 'easier' in code — that makes features less transparent to non-technical reviewers. Another difference is scope: Background applies only to scenarios in the same feature file, while hooks can be global or tagged across the entire suite. For example, logging a user in with application UI steps could be in Background for a user-focused feature, while resetting a database would be in a @Before("@database") hook. Takeaway: keep business intent visible in feature files and keep infrastructure concerns in code. Ask yourself: will a product owner care about this step? If yes, prefer Background.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Background = business-facing shared setup per feature; Hooks = technical setup/teardown across the suite. Use the product-owner test: if they care, put it in Background.

content.html:
Comparison
Background vs Hooks
A quick decision table to choose the right tool.
Background
Feature-local, business-readable steps that establish a known state before each scenario.
Hooks
Code-level lifecycle and technical setup/teardown, global or tag-scoped.
Key Takeaway

Prefer Background for stakeholder-visible setup; prefer hooks for infrastructure and cleanup. Keep responsibilities separate.

Illustrative scenarios
Business step in Background
"Given I am logged in" - visible to product owners and relevant to scenario meaning.
Technical step in Hooks
Initialize WebDriver or clear test caches - implementation detail best kept in code.
Scope difference
Background = per feature; Hooks = suite-wide or tag-scoped.

screens.title: Tag Expressions and CI: Run the Right Tests
screens.subtitle: Compose tag expressions to tailor runs in CI and local dev

narration.text: Tag expressions let you combine labels to pick exactly which scenarios to execute. Most runners support logical operators such as and, or, and not. For example, you might run all smoke tests that are not work-in-progress with an expression like @smoke and not @wip. In CI, use quick suites for commit-level feedback (for example run @smoke on pull requests) and full regression suites nightly (run @regression). A concrete workflow: on each commit run @smoke, on merge to main run @regression, and during a release candidate run a tagged @release suite. A common pitfall is creating overlapping tag semantics that make expressions ambiguous. Keep tags orthogonal — one dimension for scope (smoke vs regression), one for area (authentication vs product), and perhaps one for type (ui vs api). Another mistake is forgetting to tag new scenarios, which leaves them out of automated runs. Takeaway: define a simple tag taxonomy, document it, and wire your pipeline to run small fast suites frequently and larger suites less often. What minimal set of tags will give you fast feedback while preserving full coverage on a schedule?

keyIdea.title: CI strategy
keyIdea.text: Use simple, orthogonal tag taxonomy and run small fast tag-filtered suites in CI with larger suites scheduled less frequently.

content.html:
Process Flow
Tag Expressions and CI
Compose tags to tailor runs for speed and coverage.
Commit-level
Run @smoke on each push to catch regressions quickly.
Nightly
Run @regression overnight for broader coverage.
Release
Run full suites or tagged release checks before production deploys.
Example CLI
--tags "@smoke and not @wip"
Key Takeaway

Design a small, orthogonal tag taxonomy and map it to CI stages to balance speed and coverage.

screens.title: Directory Structure and Feature Organization
screens.subtitle: Group features and step definitions by domain to improve discoverability

narration.text: A consistent directory layout prevents chaos as features multiply. The recommended approach is to mirror your application's bounded contexts or modules: authentication features and step definitions in an authentication folder, product features in a product folder, and so on. This reduces merge conflicts, lets teams work in isolated areas, and helps new contributors find relevant specs. A concrete example: place ProductSearch. feature and ProductDetails. feature under features/product, and their step definitions under steps/product or a similarly named package. A common misconception is dumping all features into a flat directory; that makes navigation and ownership harder. Another mistake is mixing unrelated step definitions, which can cause accidental reuse or confusion about responsibilities. Takeaway: choose a structure that reflects your team's ownership boundaries and enforce it with simple repository guidelines. When reorganizing, keep tags and Backgrounds intact, and update any CI paths that depend on file locations. Which directory structure will make tests easier to find and maintain for your team? Directory Structure and Feature Organization means mirror application domains in your feature and steps directories to improve ownership and discoverability.. In practical terms, group features and step definitions by domain to improve discoverability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Organisation principle
keyIdea.text: Mirror application domains in your feature and steps directories to improve ownership and discoverability.

content.html:
Definition
Directory Structure
Group features and step definitions by bounded context to reduce collisions and ease discovery.
Example layout
features/authentication, features/product, steps/authentication, steps/product
Key Takeaway

Organize by domain and keep step definitions nearby; enforce structure with a README so contributors follow it.

Practical tips
Ownership
Assign folders to teams so they can maintain their features and steps.
Avoid cross-cutting step misuse
If a step is genuinely cross-domain, keep it in a shared steps package with clear naming.
Update CI paths
When moving files, update any CI configuration that selects features by path.

screens.title: Activity: Convert Two Features with Background and Tags
screens.subtitle: Apply Background and tags to ProductSearch and ProductDetails features

narration.text: In this hands-on activity you will create two feature files and a simple hooks class. Both ProductSearch. feature and ProductDetails. feature require the user to start on the Product Catalog page. Add a Background step to both features to remove repetition. Tag the critical scenarios with @smoke and comprehensive checks with @regression. Next, implement a Hooks class that prints messages before and after each scenario and initializes the browser for @ui tagged features. This mirrors a realistic refactor: move shared human steps into Background, tag scenarios for CI selection, and place technical initialization in a hook. A common trap is to put the 'go to catalog' navigation in hooks; avoid that because it is user-facing setup. Another trap is forgetting to add @ui to features that need browser initialization, which leads to missing setup. Takeaway: this exercise makes the separation of responsibilities concrete. After completing the files, run your runner with a tag filter such as "@smoke and not @wip" to confirm only the intended scenarios execute. What changed in your test runtime after adding these tags and Background steps?

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Hooks template
A minimal example to support the activity with safe initialization and teardown.
Key Takeaway

Keep hooks small and focused; check scenario status in the after hook and always clean up resources.

import io.cucumber.java.After;
import io.cucumber.java.Before;
import io.cucumber.java.Scenario;

public class CommonHooks {

  @Before
  public void beforeScenario(Scenario scenario) {
    System.out.println("--- Starting scenario: " + scenario.getName() + " ---");
  }

  @Before("@ui")
  public void setupUI() {
    System.out.println("Initializing browser for UI tests...");
    // Initialize WebDriver here for @ui scenarios
  }

  @After
  public void afterScenario(Scenario scenario) {
    System.out.println("--- Finished scenario: " + scenario.getName() + " with status: " + scenario.getStatus() + " ---");
    // Cleanup resources to avoid leaks
  }
}

screens.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Guidelines to keep your Gherkin suite maintainable and reliable

narration.text: Maintaining a BDD suite is an ongoing activity; here are compact best practices to reduce technical debt. First, keep Background short and business-focused. If removing a step changes scenario meaning, it probably belongs in the scenario. Second, use tags sparingly and orthogonally — separate execution intent (smoke/regression) from domain (authentication/product) and layer (ui/api). Third, place infrastructure initialization and cleanup in hooks, never in Background; this keeps feature files readable for non-developers. Fourth, organize files by bounded context to reduce collisions and improve ownership. Fifth, always ensure @After hooks reliably clean up resources to prevent flaky tests due to shared state. Common mistakes include overusing Background to hide behavior, scattering tags without documentation, and failing to scope heavy initialization so CI runs unnecessary work. A practical rule: adopt a small tag set, document it in the repo README, and add a quick CI mapping so everyone knows which tags run where. Takeaway: clarity and separation of concerns reduce fragility and make tests a reliable communication tool between developers and stakeholders. Which of these practices will you apply first to reduce flakiness?

keyIdea.title: Practice checklist
keyIdea.text: Keep Background minimal, scope hooks, use a small tag set, organize by domain, and ensure reliable cleanup to avoid flaky tests.

content.html:
Best Practices
Keep tests clear and isolated
A short checklist to prevent common issues as your suite scales.
  • Background: only shared business preconditions
  • Hooks: technical setup/teardown and tagged initialization
  • Tags: small, orthogonal taxonomies
  • Structure: mirror application domains for discoverability
  • Cleanup: always release resources in @After hooks
Common mistake
Using hooks to hide business steps that stakeholders need to read in the feature files.
Pro tip
Maintain a README that documents tag meanings and CI mappings so the team uses tags consistently.
Key Takeaway

Separation of concerns plus a small set of conventions keeps BDD suites readable and fast.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to carry forward

narration.text: These three concise concept cards summarize the chapter's most important ideas. First, Tags are labels used to categorize and selectively execute scenarios; use them to speed CI and scope hooks. Second, Background is for shared, business-readable setup within a single feature file; keep it minimal so it does not hide scenario intent. Third, Hooks are code-level lifecycle methods for technical initialization and cleanup, and they can be tagged to run only when needed. Together, these tools separate concerns: Background keeps features readable for stakeholders; hooks keep technical details in code; tags let you choose which tests to run. A common pitfall is mixing these responsibilities: putting business steps in hooks or infrastructure steps in Background. Your practical next steps are to adopt a small tag taxonomy, refactor repeated steps into Background only when appropriate, and move technical setup into tagged hooks with reliable cleanup. How will you apply these ideas in your next test refactor?

keyIdea.title: Memory hooks
keyIdea.text: Tags = selection, Background = readable setup, Hooks = technical lifecycle. Use each for its intended responsibility.

content.html:

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to guide your work

narration.text: Keep these three reminders close as you refactor or author new features. First, ask whether a setup step is about business intent or technical detail — if it’s business intent, place it in Background; if it’s technical, place it in hooks. Second, adopt a small, documented tag vocabulary so CI and developers have predictable filters to run. Third, organize feature files and step definitions by domain to promote ownership and reduce merge conflicts. A small, consistent set of habits will prevent many common problems: hidden preconditions, slow CI, and resource leaks. After you finish this chapter, pick one feature to refactor using these rules and observe the difference in readability and runtime. Which one will you choose first? What to Remember means decide between background and hooks by stakeholder visibility, use tags with discipline, and organize files by domain.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to guide your work. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Final memory
keyIdea.text: Decide between Background and hooks by stakeholder visibility, use tags with discipline, and organize files by domain.

content.html:
What to Remember
Decide by visibility
Business steps → Background; technical steps → Hooks.
Tag discipline
Use a small, documented set for CI mapping and clarity.
Organize by domain
Mirror application contexts in folders and step packages.
Final takeaway

Small conventions and separation of concerns make BDD tests a reliable communication tool and a practical automation asset.
